Develop a Measurable Cooling as a Service Offering

Thematic Area: Cooling Services & Energy Efficiency

How might we deliver reliable cooling through a service model with clear performance standards, ownership responsibilities and customer economics?

Background

An Indonesian solar EPC business has identified Cooling as a Service as a technology and business-model interest to complement its energy offering.

The objective is to develop a model in which customers pay for agreed cooling services with clear equipment ownership, maintenance and performance responsibilities. Relevant partners provide efficient cooling equipment, controls, metering, asset finance and service operations.

The collaboration will connect a suitable customer application with the equipment, funding and operating model needed to deliver measurable cooling performance.

Significance of Problem

Without an effective solution, the challenges include:

  • Slower offering development: Unclear customer requirements and delivery responsibilities slow the development of a viable cooling service.
  • Difficult service pricing: A measured energy baseline and defined cooling output are essential for comparing costs and customer benefits.
  • Weak performance visibility: Incomplete maintenance and measurement arrangements make cooling commitments harder to manage.

Existing Efforts

  • Business direction: Cooling as a Service forms part of the business’s energy-service interests.
  • Partner roles: Bring together solar monitoring, financing-preparation and workflow tools with specialist cooling equipment and service-operation expertise.
  • Collaboration focus: Select a customer application and specialist partner. Define cooling requirements, baseline energy use, metering, maintenance and financing. Compare service payments with a conventional purchase and measure cooling quality, availability, energy use and total cost in a controlled pilot.

Potential Market Size

  • Regional demand growth: The 2026 Southeast Asia energy outlook projects residential air-conditioner stocks to triple by 2035 under current policy settings, indicating strong regional growth in cooling demand.
  • Broader service market: Global Energy as a Service revenue is forecast to reach US$222.7 billion by 2033. The market spans energy supply, maintenance and efficiency services.

Eligibility / Qualification

  • Technology readiness: Minimum technology readiness level 3 (TRL3).
  • NUS linkage: NUS student or graduate founder, or incubation through an NUS programme such as BLOCK71.
  • Local and overseas startups: Open to Indonesian and overseas startups.
  • Commitment: Complete the selection process and travel to Indonesia if selected.
